# Repair an orientation-sensitive fiber-scattering reduction

A grazing-incidence/fiber diffraction reduction was run on a detector-panel
acquisition whose fiber-axis orientation convention is recorded in the
experimental setup. The workflow completes, but changing that supported
acquisition setting produces a reciprocal-space observation whose movement is
inconsistent with the supplied scattering geometry for an asymmetric panel.
That makes it difficult to interpret whether observed features are in-plane or
out-of-plane.

Use the supplied offline source, scientific material, and reproduction
workbench to investigate the discrepancy and repair the implementation. The
orientation value in this task belongs to the project's Fiber/sample-axis
workflow; it is not the separate detector metadata enum. The repair must work
for the supported Fiber orientation conventions generally, not only for the
provided panel. Do not modify task metadata, fixtures, the public runner, or
the evaluation harness. Place your solution in `<patch-omitted>`.

scattering geometry for an asymmetric detector panel. Use the offline source,

# Public reproduction

Run the following command from the task root:

```bash
python reproduce.py
```

The command constructs a deterministic detector-panel reduction using the
provided acquisition fixture and the project's normal worker-facing Fiber
workflow. It reports a small set of scientific observations from two
representations of the same acquisition. It writes the same JSON report to
`outputs/public_reproduction_report.json`.

Report states:

- `workflow_completed`: a usable observation was produced. Compare the two
  recorded runs and inspect whether their feature locations and coordinate
  extents move in a way that is consistent with the supplied scattering
  geometry. The angle view and reciprocal-polar view are two representations
  of the same physical scattering observation, not separate reference
  answers.
- `runner_failure`: an import, fixture, path, or other execution problem
  prevented the scientific workflow from running.

This is a public workbench rather than the complete grading oracle. A repair
that changes the report for this one panel may still fail broader evaluation;
the public report intentionally does not state a corrected numerical answer.
# Scientific material: detector orientation in fiber and grazing-incidence scattering

## Project and method references

The supplied source snapshot is from the pyFAI scientific-computing project.
Its project paper is:

- J. Kieffer and G. Ashiotis, *pyFAI: a Python library for high performance
  azimuthal integration*, Journal of Applied Crystallography 48 (2015),
  510--519. DOI: <https://doi.org/10.1107/S1600576715004306>.

The matching source revision also includes the project's Fiber/Grazing-Incidence
user tutorial. It describes a workflow in which a detector image is reduced to
in-plane/out-of-plane reciprocal coordinates, exit angles, or polar
coordinates. The relevant acquisition settings are the Fiber/sample-axis
orientation convention, incident angle, and tilt angle. The orientation value
is the project's Fiber-workflow convention for the in-plane axes; it must not
be confused with the separate detector metadata enum used by some image
loaders. All angles in the supplied case are in radians.

## Scattering-vector interpretation

Let `k_i` be the incident wave vector and `k_f` the wave vector directed from
the sample to a detector location. The momentum-transfer or scattering vector
is

\[
\mathbf q = \mathbf k_f - \mathbf k_i.
\]

Detector geometry determines the direction of `k_f`. A reciprocal-space map is
therefore a coordinate transformation of an experimental detector location,
not just a relabelled image. Different displayed components, exit angles, and
polar quantities are supported representations of the same physical scattering
geometry.

## Acquisition frames

The Fiber/sample-axis orientation setting states which in-plane axes and
handedness were used to interpret an acquisition. The supported conventions
include identity, reflections, half turns, and quarter turns. It is
consequently meaningful for the same array index under two recorded
orientations to refer to different directions in the Fiber coordinate frame.
A non-centrosymmetric panel makes this effect visible. This convention is
distinct from the detector metadata enum: the task concerns the value passed
through the Fiber reduction workflow.

The incident and tilt settings describe rotations of the sample reference used
for grazing-incidence/fiber work. Rigid rotations redistribute vector
components while preserving the vector magnitude. This gives useful checks:
the Fiber-plane orientation convention is applied to the detector-plane axes
before those sample-reference rotations, and the coordinate representation may
change while it continues to describe one physically consistent scattering
vector.

## Experimental consequence

In a grazing-incidence or fiber experiment, in-plane and out-of-plane feature
positions are used to interpret sample orientation and structure. A calculation
that completes while ignoring a recorded Fiber orientation can reflect or
misplace a feature in reciprocal space. The supplied panel is a small,
deterministic workbench for investigating that class of discrepancy; it is not
a complete reference answer.

The task is fully offline. The paper URLs are citations only; all material
needed to run and investigate the supplied experiment is local.

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Any

import numpy as np


def _panel_coordinates(panel: dict[str, Any]) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
    rows = int(panel["rows"])
    columns = int(panel["columns"])
    pixel_size = float(panel["pixel_size_m"])
    row_index, column_index = np.indices((rows, columns), dtype=np.float64)
    horizontal = (column_index - float(panel["beam_column"])) * pixel_size
    vertical = (float(panel["beam_row"]) - row_index) * pixel_size
    distance = np.full_like(horizontal, float(panel["sample_to_panel_m"]))
    return horizontal, vertical, distance


def _signal(panel: dict[str, Any], signal: dict[str, Any]) -> np.ndarray:
    row_index, column_index = np.indices((int(panel["rows"]), int(panel["columns"])), dtype=np.float64)
    intensity = np.full(row_index.shape, float(signal["background"]), dtype=np.float64)
    for feature in signal["features"]:
        squared_distance = (row_index - float(feature["row"])) ** 2 + (column_index - float(feature["column"])) ** 2
        intensity += float(feature["amplitude"]) * np.exp(-squared_distance / (2.0 * float(feature["sigma_pixels"]) ** 2))
    return intensity


def _run_reduction(
    intensity: np.ndarray,
    panel: dict[str, Any],
    acquisition: dict[str, Any],
    orientation: int,
) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Run the normal pyFAI worker workflow on one recorded acquisition."""
    from pyFAI.integrator.fiber import FiberIntegrator
    from pyFAI.worker import WorkerFiber

    pixel_size = float(panel["pixel_size_m"])
    integrator = FiberIntegrator(
        dist=float(panel["sample_to_panel_m"]),
        poni1=float(panel["beam_row"]) * pixel_size,
        poni2=float(panel["beam_column"]) * pixel_size,
        pixel1=pixel_size,
        pixel2=pixel_size,
        wavelength=float(acquisition["wavelength_m"]),
    )
    npt_ip = max(8, min(int(panel["columns"]), 32))
    npt_oop = max(8, min(int(panel["rows"]), 32))

    # Use the worker-facing path used by pyFAI applications. The two views
    # are configured as separate experiments so this workbench exposes an
    # observable workflow rather than a unit-conversion adapter.
    angle_worker = WorkerFiber(
        fiberIntegrator=integrator,
        npt_ip=npt_ip,
        npt_oop=npt_oop,
        unit_ip="exit_angle_horz_rad",
        unit_oop="exit_angle_vert_rad",
        incident_angle=float(acquisition["incident_angle_rad"]),
        tilt_angle=float(acquisition["tilt_angle_rad"]),
        sample_orientation=orientation,
        method=("no", "histogram", "python"),
    )
    angle_worker.correct_solid_angle = False
    angle_worker.output = "raw"
    angle_result = angle_worker.process(intensity)

    polar_worker = WorkerFiber(
        fiberIntegrator=FiberIntegrator(
            dist=float(panel["sample_to_panel_m"]),
            poni1=float(panel["beam_row"]) * pixel_size,
            poni2=float(panel["beam_column"]) * pixel_size,
            pixel1=pixel_size,
            pixel2=pixel_size,
            wavelength=float(acquisition["wavelength_m"]),
        ),
        npt_ip=npt_ip,
        npt_oop=npt_oop,
        unit_ip="qtot_nm^-1",
        unit_oop="chigi_rad",
        incident_angle=float(acquisition["incident_angle_rad"]),
        tilt_angle=float(acquisition["tilt_angle_rad"]),
        sample_orientation=orientation,
        method=("no", "histogram", "python"),
    )
    polar_worker.correct_solid_angle = False
    polar_worker.output = "raw"
    polar_result = polar_worker.process(intensity)

    def summarize(result: Any) -> dict[str, Any]:
        first_axis = np.asarray(result.inplane, dtype=np.float64)
        second_axis = np.asarray(result.outofplane, dtype=np.float64)
        reduced = np.asarray(result.intensity, dtype=np.float64)
        if not (
            np.isfinite(first_axis).all()
            and np.isfinite(second_axis).all()
            and np.isfinite(reduced).all()
        ):
            raise ValueError("the detector-panel reduction produced a non-finite observation")

        positive = np.maximum(reduced, 0.0)
        total = float(np.sum(positive))
        if total <= 0.0:
            raise ValueError("the detector panel has no usable intensity")
        first_weights = np.sum(positive, axis=0)
        second_weights = np.sum(positive, axis=1)
        return {
            "shape": [int(value) for value in reduced.shape],
            "coordinate_extent": [
                [float(np.min(first_axis)), float(np.max(first_axis))],
                [float(np.min(second_axis)), float(np.max(second_axis))],
            ],
            "feature_center": [
                float(np.sum(first_axis * first_weights) / total),
                float(np.sum(second_axis * second_weights) / total),
            ],
            "occupied_fraction": float(np.count_nonzero(positive) / positive.size),
        }

    return {
        "angle_view": summarize(angle_result),
        "reciprocal_polar_view": summarize(polar_result),
    }


def run_panel_experiment(case: dict[str, Any]) -> dict[str, object]:
    panel = case["panel"]
    acquisition = case["acquisition"]
    intensity = _signal(panel, case["signal"])
    run_a = _run_reduction(
        intensity, panel, acquisition, int(acquisition["orientation_a"])
    )
    run_b = _run_reduction(
        intensity, panel, acquisition, int(acquisition["orientation_b"])
    )
    return {
        "panel_shape": [int(panel["rows"]), int(panel["columns"])],
        "run_a": run_a,
        "run_b": run_b,
    }

201	        :param incident_angle: tilting of the sample towards the beam (analog to rot2): in radians
202	        :param tilt_angle: tilting of the sample orthogonal to the beam direction (analog to rot3): in radians
203	        :param int sample_orientation: 1-8, orientation of the fiber axis according to EXIF orientation values (see def sample_orientation)
204	        :param str filename: output filename in 2/3 column ascii format
205	        :param bool correctSolidAngle: correct for solid angle of each pixel if True
206	        :param ndarray mask: array (same size as image) with 1 for masked pixels, and 0 for valid pixels
207	        :param float dummy: value for dead/masked pixels

211	                * None for no correction,
212	                * True for using the former correction
213	        :param ndarray dark: dark noise image
214	        :param ndarray flat: flat field image
215	        :param IntegrationMethod method: IntegrationMethod instance or 3-tuple with (splitting, algorithm, implementation)
216	        :param float normalization_factor: Value of a normalization monitor

218	        :return: chi bins center positions and regrouped intensity
219	        :rtype: Integrate1dResult

221	        deprecated_params = get_deprecated_params_1d(**kwargs)
222	        npt_oop = deprecated_params.get('npt_oop', None) or npt_oop
223	        npt_ip = deprecated_params.get('npt_ip', None) or npt_ip
224	        unit_oop = deprecated_params.get('unit_oop', None) or unit_oop
225	        unit_ip = deprecated_params.get('unit_ip', None) or unit_ip
226	        oop_range = deprecated_params.get('oop_range', None) or oop_range
227	        ip_range = deprecated_params.get('ip_range', None) or ip_range
228	        vertical_integration = deprecated_params.get('vertical_integration', None) or vertical_integration
229	
230	        invalid_keys = [k for k in kwargs if any(ss in k for ss in ["oop", "ip", "unit", "range"])]
231	        if invalid_keys:
232	            logger.warning(f"""Key parameters {invalid_keys} are wrong or deprecated.
233	                            Valid parameters: npt_ip, unit_ip, ip_range, npt_oop, unit_oop, oop_range""")
234	
235	        unit_ip = unit_ip or 'qip_nm^-1'
236	        unit_oop = unit_oop or 'qoop_nm^-1'
237	        incident_angle = kwargs.get('incident_angle', None)
238	        tilt_angle = kwargs.get('tilt_angle', None)
239	
240	        angle_unit_parsed = to_unit(angle_unit, ANGLE_UNITS)
241	
242	        if incident_angle is not None:
243	            incident_angle = (incident_angle % angle_unit_parsed.period) / angle_unit_parsed.scale
244	        if tilt_angle is not None:
245	            tilt_angle = (tilt_angle % angle_unit_parsed.period) / angle_unit_parsed.scale
246	
247	        unit_ip = parse_fiber_unit(unit=unit_ip,
248	                                   incident_angle=incident_angle,
249	                                   tilt_angle=tilt_angle,
250	                                   sample_orientation=sample_orientation)
251	        unit_oop = parse_fiber_unit(unit=unit_oop,
252	                                    incident_angle=unit_ip.incident_angle,
253	                                    tilt_angle=unit_ip.tilt_angle,
254	                                    sample_orientation=unit_ip.sample_orientation)
255	
256	        self.reset_integrator(incident_angle=unit_ip.incident_angle,
257	                              tilt_angle=unit_ip.tilt_angle,
258	                              sample_orientation=unit_ip.sample_orientation)
259	
260	        if (isinstance(method, (tuple, list)) and method[0] != "no") or (isinstance(method, IntegrationMethod) and method.split != "no"):
261	            logger.warning(f"Method {method} is using a pixel-splitting scheme. GI integration should be use WITHOUT PIXEL-SPLITTING! The results could be wrong!")
262	
263	        if vertical_integration and npt_oop is None:
264	            raise RuntimeError("npt_oop (out-of-plane bins) is needed to do the integration")
265	        elif not vertical_integration and npt_ip is None:
266	            raise RuntimeError("npt_ip (in-plane bins) is needed to do the integration")
267	
268	        npt_ip = npt_ip or 1000
269	        npt_oop = npt_oop or 1000
270	
271	        res2d_fiber = self.integrate2d_fiber(data,
272	                                  npt_ip=npt_ip, unit_ip=unit_ip, ip_range=ip_range,
273	                                  npt_oop=npt_oop, unit_oop=unit_oop, oop_range=oop_range,
274	                                  sample_orientation=sample_orientation,
275	                                  filename=None,
276	                                  correctSolidAngle=correctSolidAngle,
277	                                  mask=mask, dummy=dummy, delta_dummy=delta_dummy,
278	                                  polarization_factor=polarization_factor,
279	                                  dark=dark, flat=flat, method=method,
280	                                  normalization_factor=normalization_factor,
281	                                  **kwargs)
282	
283	        if vertical_integration:
284	            output_unit = res2d_fiber.oop_unit
285	            integration_axis = -1
286	            integrated_vector = res2d_fiber.outofplane
287	        else:
288	            output_unit = res2d_fiber.ip_unit
289	            integration_axis = -2
290	            integrated_vector = res2d_fiber.inplane
291	
292	        sum_signal = res2d_fiber.sum_signal.sum(axis=integration_axis)
293	        count = res2d_fiber.count.sum(axis=integration_axis)
294	        sum_normalization = res2d_fiber._sum_normalization.sum(axis=integration_axis)
295	        mask_ = numpy.where(count == 0)
296	        empty = dummy if dummy is not None else self._empty
297	        if USE_NUMEXPR:
298	            intensity = numexpr.evaluate("where(sum_normalization <= 0, 0.0, sum_signal / sum_normalization)")
299	        else:
300	            intensity = numpy.where(sum_normalization <= 0, 0.0, sum_signal / sum_normalization)
301	        intensity[mask_] = empty
302	
303	        if res2d_fiber.sigma is not None:
304	            sum_variance = res2d_fiber.sum_variance.sum(axis=integration_axis)
305	            if USE_NUMEXPR:
306	                sigma = numexpr.evaluate("where(sum_normalization <= 0, 0.0, sqrt(sum_variance) / sum_normalization)")
307	            else:
308	                sigma = numpy.where(sum_normalization <= 0, 0.0, numpy.sqrt(sum_variance) / sum_normalization)
309	            sigma[mask_] = empty
310	        else:
311	            sum_variance = None
312	            sigma = None
313	
314	        result = Integrate1dFiberResult(integrated_vector, intensity, sigma)
315	        result._set_vertical_integration(vertical_integration)
316	        result._set_method_called("integrate_radial")
317	        result._set_unit(output_unit)
318	        result._set_sum_normalization(sum_normalization)
319	        result._set_count(count)
320	        result._set_sum_signal(sum_signal)
321	        result._set_sum_variance(sum_variance)
322	        result._set_has_dark_correction(dark is not None)

326	        result._set_method = res2d_fiber.method
327	        result._set_compute_engine = res2d_fiber.compute_engine
328	
329	        if filename is not None:
330	            save_integrate_result(filename, result)
331	
332	        return result

591	def get_missing_wedge_threshold(intensity:numpy.ndarray, threshold_bins=None) -> float:
592	    """Calculate the count threshold to mask the missing wedge.
593	
594	    :param intensity numpy.ndarray: 2d array with the bin-wise normalization values
595	    :param threshold_bins: number of bins to histogram the normalization values, defaults to max(intensity.shape)
596	
597	    Returns:
598	        float: The count threshold to mask the missing wedge

987	    6 - Image is rotated 90 degrees counter clockwise
988	    7 - Image is mirrored and rotated 90 degrees clockwise
989	    8 - Image is rotated 90 degrees clockwise

991	    if sample_orientation == 1:
992	        hpos = x
993	        vpos = y
994	    elif sample_orientation == 2:
995	        hpos = -x
996	        vpos = y
997	    elif sample_orientation == 3:
998	        hpos = -x
999	        vpos = -y
1000	    elif sample_orientation == 4:
1001	        hpos = x
1002	        vpos = -y
1003	    elif sample_orientation == 5:
1004	        hpos = -y
1005	        vpos = -x
1006	    elif sample_orientation == 6:
1007	        hpos = -y

1011	        vpos = x
1012	    elif sample_orientation == 8:

Important detail: `center_array` caches by `key = f"{unit.space}_center"`. `unit.space` is derived from `unit.name`: `"_".join(name.split("_")[:-1])`. For `exit_angle_horz_rad`, space = "exit_angle_horz". For `qip_nm^-1`, space = "qip_nm"? Let's compute: "qip_nm^-1".split("_") -> ["qip", "nm^-1"], join all but last = "qip". Hmm `"_".join([...][:-1])` for 2 parts gives "qip". For "qtot_nm^-1" → "qtot". For "chigi_rad" → "chigi". So cache keys differ among units mostly.

But note: `to_unit(unit)` is called at start of `center_array`. When passed a UnitFiber instance, `Unit.parse` with type_=None uses ANY_UNITS dict: `if isinstance(obj, (str,))` only for str; elif isinstance(obj, (Unit, UnitFiber)): rad_unit = obj. OK it returns the same instance.

Now, for the center array, the fiber unit's equation is called with 7 args: x, y, z, wavelength, incident_angle, tilt_angle, sample_orientation. In `UnitFiber._update_ne_equation`, `ne_equation` signature: `def ne_equation(x, y, z=None, wavelength=None, incident_angle=self._incident_angle, tilt_angle=self._tilt_angle, sample_orientation=self._sample_orientation, ne_formula=ne_formula)`. Then it sets `π = PI; λ = wavelength; η = self._incident_angle; χ = self._tilt_angle`. It ignores passed incident_angle/tilt_angle/sample_orientation args, using instance values. Fine.

But here's a potential bug: When `_update_ne_equation` is called, it computes `signature = [(key, numpy.float64) for key in "xyzλπηχ" if key in self.formula]`. Then `ne_formula = numexpr.NumExpr(self.formula, signature)`. The formula after replacement may contain variables. Then `args = tuple(ldict[i] for i in ne_formula.input_names)`. It sets λ, η, χ. For formulas containing π, ldict has π. OK.

But the problem: `formula` is mutated in place, and `formula_so1` is stored. For orientation changes on the same unit instance, `formula_so1` remains the original formula; OK.

But there's a bigger issue: In `_update_ne_equation` for orientation 2, `formula_ = self.formula_so1.replace("x", "(-x)")`. This changes `x` in the formula, but if the formula contains `x` in e.g. `exp`? no. But wait: the formulas for qip etc. contain strings like `((({formula_qhorz_rot} > 0) * 2) - 1)`. That's fine.

However, the string replace might inadvertently modify `λ`? No.

Wait, the actual reported run B doesn't match a horizontal flip. Let's test whether run B corresponds to vertical flip (y->-y) or something else. Let's compute the expected extents from numpy equations directly.

Actually first, let me see if there is a discrepancy between the `formula` string replacement and the `rotate_sample_orientation` numpy function for orientations 5-8. Look closely at orientation 5 string replacement:

```
formula_ = self.formula_so1
formula_ = formula_.replace("x", "ψ").replace("y", "ξ")
formula_ = formula_.replace("ψ", "(-y)").replace("ξ", "(-x)")
```

This yields x→-y, y→-x, which matches rotate_sample_orientation 5: hpos=-y, vpos=-x. OK.

Orientation 6: x→-y, y→x; rotate 6: hpos=-y, vpos=x. OK.
Orientation 7: x→y, y→x; rotate 7: hpos=y, vpos=x. OK.
Orientation 8: x→y, y→-x; rotate 8: hpos=y, vpos=-x. OK.

So the formula replacement is consistent.

But wait, the formulas have a subtlety: the x/y replacements change *all* occurrences, including inside the exit angle formulas where x is also inside `formula_x_rot_iangle = "x"` etc. Fine.

Now let's compute what run B actually did. Maybe the bug is not in units.py string replacement but in `WorkerFiber`, which might pass `sample_orientation` to the wrong place, or the cache (`_cached_array` keyed by `unit.space`) reuses stale arrays when changing sample orientation. Aha! That's a strong candidate. The `Geometry` object caches center/corner arrays by `f"{unit.space}_center"` / `f"{unit.space}_corner"` without including sample_orientation, incident_angle, or tilt_angle in the key. In `_run_reduction`, the workflow creates a new FiberIntegrator for each run, so cache is fresh. But the polar_worker and angle_worker within each run use separate integrators. Hmm, within one integrator, angle_worker.process then polar_worker.process use separate integrators (the polar worker creates a new FiberIntegrator). So cache reuse across orientation changes is not happening in this workflow. But in general pyFAI usage, reset_integrator calls `self.reset()` which clears `_cached_array`. So probably fine.

Let's look at WorkerFiber to see what it does with sample_orientation.

events.text:
WorkerFiber process passes unit_ip/unit_oop to integrate2d_ng. In `integrate2d_ng`, radial_unit, azimuth_unit = unit; then `radial_unit = units.to_unit(radial_unit, units.RADIAL_UNITS)` and azimuth_unit = units.to_unit(azimuth_unit, units.AZIMUTHAL_UNITS). Wait! `to_unit(radial_unit, units.RADIAL_UNITS)` might break the UnitFiber instance? Let's inspect `Unit.parse`: if obj is instance of Unit or UnitFiber, rad_unit = obj (ignores type_). So fine.

Then it uses `unit` (tuple) later. Let me inspect integrate2d_ng to see if there is a `get_config_shared` issue or something.

def lab_q(h,v,z,lam):
    sv = np.arctan2(v, np.sqrt(z**2+h**2))
    sh = np.arctan2(h, z)
    qb = 2.0e-9*np.pi/lam*(np.cos(sv)*np.cos(sh)-1.0)
    qh = 2.0e-9*np.pi/lam*np.cos(sv)*np.sin(sh)
    qv = 2.0e-9*np.pi/lam*np.sin(sv)
    return qb,qh,qv

def sample_q(h,v,z,lam,inc,tilt):
    qb,qh,qv = lab_q(h,v,z,lam)
    ci_,si_ = np.cos(inc),np.sin(inc)
    ct,st = np.cos(tilt),np.sin(tilt)
    # R_inc
    b2 = ci_*qb + si_*qv
    h2 = qh
    v2 = -si_*qb + ci_*qv
    # R_tilt (x axis)
    b3 = b2
    h3 = ct*h2 + st*v2
    v3 = -st*h2 + ct*v2
    return b3,h3,v3

    b3,h3,v3 = sample_q(h,v,z,lam,inc,tilt)

    return qip, v3

"""Unique place where the version number is defined.

provides:
* version = "1.2.3" or "1.2.3-beta4"
* version_info = named tuple (1,2,3,"beta",4)
* hexversion: 0x010203B4
* strictversion = "1.2.3b4
* debianversion = "1.2.3~beta4"
* calc_hexversion: the function to transform a version_tuple into an integer

This is called hexversion since it only really looks meaningful when viewed as the
result of passing it to the built-in hex() function.
The version_info value may be used for a more human-friendly encoding of the same information.

The hexversion is a 32-bit number with the following layout:
Bits (big endian order)     Meaning
1-8     PY_MAJOR_VERSION (the 2 in 2.1.0a3)
9-16     PY_MINOR_VERSION (the 1 in 2.1.0a3)
17-24     PY_MICRO_VERSION (the 0 in 2.1.0a3)
25-28     PY_RELEASE_LEVEL (0xA for alpha, 0xB for beta, 0xC for release candidate and 0xF for final)
29-32     PY_RELEASE_SERIAL (the 3 in 2.1.0a3, zero for final releases)

Thus 2.1.0a3 is hexversion 0x020100a3.

"""

__authors__ = ["Jérôme Kieffer", "V. Valls"]
__license__ = "MIT"
__copyright__ = "European Synchrotron Radiation Facility, Grenoble, France"
__date__ = "19/12/2025"
__status__ = "production"
__docformat__ = 'restructuredtext'
__all__ = ["date", "version_info", "strictversion", "hexversion", "debianversion",
           "calc_hexversion", "citation"]


from collections import namedtuple


RELEASE_LEVEL_VALUE = {"dev": 0,
                       "alpha": 10,
                       "beta": 11,
                       "gamma": 12,
                       "rc": 13,
                       "final": 15}
MAJOR = 2026
MINOR = 1
MICRO = 0
RELEV = "dev"  # <16
SERIAL = 0  # <16

date = __date__

_version_info = namedtuple("version_info", ["major", "minor", "micro", "releaselevel", "serial"])
version_info = _version_info(MAJOR, MINOR, MICRO, RELEV, SERIAL)

strictversion = version = debianversion = "%d.%d.%d" % version_info[:3]
if version_info.releaselevel != "final":
    version += "-%s%s" % version_info[-2:]
    debianversion += "~adev%i" % version_info[-1] if RELEV == "dev" else "~%s%i" % version_info[-2:]
    prerel = "a" if RELEASE_LEVEL_VALUE.get(version_info[3], 0) < 10 else "b"
    if prerel not in "ab":
        prerel = "a"
    strictversion += prerel + str(version_info[-1])

_PATTERN = None


def calc_hexversion(major=0, minor=0, micro=0, releaselevel="dev", serial=0, string=None):
    """Calculate the hexadecimal version number from the tuple version_info:

    :param major: integer
    :param minor: integer
    :param micro: integer
    :param relev: integer or string
    :param serial: integer
    :param string: version number as a string
    :return: integer always increasing with revision numbers
    """
    if string is not None:
        global _PATTERN
        if _PATTERN is None:
            import re
            _PATTERN = re.compile(r"(\d+)\.(\d+)\.(\d+)(\w+)?$")
        result = _PATTERN.match(string)
        if result is None:
            raise ValueError("'%s' is not a valid version" % string)
        result = result.groups()
        major, minor, micro = int(result[0]), int(result[1]), int(result[2])
        releaselevel = result[3]
        if releaselevel is None:
            releaselevel = 0

    try:
        releaselevel = int(releaselevel)
    except ValueError:
        releaselevel = RELEASE_LEVEL_VALUE.get(releaselevel, 0)

    hex_version = int(serial)
    hex_version |= releaselevel * 1 << 4
    hex_version |= int(micro) * 1 << 8
    hex_version |= int(minor) * 1 << 16
    hex_version |= int(major) * 1 << 24
    return hex_version


hexversion = calc_hexversion(*version_info)

citation = "doi:10.1107/S1600576715004306"

if __name__ == "__main__":

    options = parser.parse_args()
    if options.debian:
        print(debianversion)
    elif options.wheel:
        print(strictversion)
    else:
        print(version)

EPS32=1.0+np.finfo(np.float32).eps

def reference(panel,acq,sig,so):
    rows,cols=int(panel['rows']),int(panel['columns'])
    ps=float(panel['pixel_size_m']); brow=float(panel['beam_row']); bcol=float(panel['beam_column']); dist=float(panel['sample_to_panel_m'])
    lam=float(acq['wavelength_m']); inc=float(acq['incident_angle_rad']); tilt=float(acq['tilt_angle_rad'])
    I=_signal(panel,sig)
    ri,ci=np.indices((rows,cols),dtype=np.float64)
    x=(ci+0.5)*ps-bcol*ps; y=(ri+0.5)*ps-brow*ps; z=np.full_like(x,dist)
    def rot(x,y,so):
        if so==1: return x,y
        if so==2: return -x,y
        if so==3: return -x,-y
        if so==4: return x,-y
        if so==5: return -y,-x
        if so==6: return -y,x
        if so==7: return y,x
        if so==8: return y,-x

    ci_,si_=np.cos(inc),np.sin(inc); ct,st=np.cos(tilt),np.sin(tilt)
    xi=h; yi=v*ci_-z*si_; zi=v*si_+z*ci_
    xt=xi*ct-yi*st; yt=xi*st+yi*ct; zt=zi
    eh=np.arctan2(xt,zt); ev=np.arctan2(yt,np.sqrt(zt*zt+xt*xt))
    # q components
    sv=np.arctan2(v,np.sqrt(z*z+h*h)); sh=np.arctan2(h,z)

    qh=2.0e-9*np.pi/lam*np.cos(sv)*np.sin(sh)
    qv=2.0e-9*np.pi/lam*np.sin(sv)
    b1=ci_*qb+si_*qv; h1=qh; v1=-si_*qb+ci_*qv
    b2=b1; h2=ct*h1-st*v1; v2=st*h1+ct*v1
    qip=np.sqrt(b2*b2+h2*h2)*np.sign(h2); qoop=v2
    qt=4.0e-9*np.pi*np.sin(np.arctan2(np.sqrt(h*h+v*v),z)/2.0)/lam
    chi=np.arctan2(qip,qoop)
    npt_ip=max(8,min(cols,32)); npt_oop=max(8,min(rows,32))
    def hist(rad,azim):
        H,ed1,ed2=np.histogram2d(rad.ravel(),azim.ravel(),bins=(npt_ip,npt_oop),weights=I.ravel(),range=[[rad.min(),rad.max()*EPS32],[azim.min(),azim.max()*EPS32]])
        C,_,_=np.histogram2d(rad.ravel(),azim.ravel(),bins=(npt_ip,npt_oop),weights=np.ones(I.size),range=[[rad.min(),rad.max()*EPS32],[azim.min(),azim.max()*EPS32]])
        return H.T,C.T,ed1,ed2
    out={}

I found and fixed the orientation-sensitive inconsistency. Here's a summary of the investigation and the resulting patch.

## Diagnosis

The workflow produces two representations of the same scattering geometry:

- **angle view** (`exit_angle_horz_rad` / `exit_angle_vert_rad`)
- **reciprocal-polar view** (`qtot_nm^-1` / `chigi_rad`)

Both are built from the same detector positions and the same incident/tilt rotations, so a change in the Fiber `sample_orientation` must move both views consistently.

In `pyFAI/units.py` I found that the two paths used **different tilt-rotation conventions**:

- `eq_exit_angle_vert` / `eq_exit_angle_horz` correctly use:
  - incident rotation about the horizontal axis (`x`),
  - tilt rotation about the beam axis (`z`),
  matching the documented `analog to rot2` / `analog to rot3` geometry.
- The reciprocal-space path (`rotation_tilt_angle`, `formula_qhorz_rot`, `formula_qvert_rot`, `qip`, `qoop`, `chigi`) instead used a tilt rotation with the **opposite sign** (and about the wrong effective axis).

The effect: `chigi = arctan2(qip, qoop)` was mirrored with respect to the exit-angle geometry, so changing the recorded Fiber orientation moved reciprocal-space features inconsistently and made in-plane/out-of-plane assignment ambiguous.

I also found two secondary defects in the same workflow that would break other supported usage:

1. `UnitFiber._update_ne_equation()` computed the numexpr variable signature from the *previously substituted* formula, and orientation 1 never reset the formula. Repeatedly changing a unit's orientation (or reusing a `WorkerFiber`) caused `ValueError: input names ... don't match` for units whose formulas change variable set (e.g. `scattering_angle_horz_rad`), and returning to orientation 1 kept a stale formula.
2. The pure-numpy fallback path ignored `sample_orientation` for exit/scattering-angle units and used `math.cos`/`math.sin` on arrays in the `q_lab_*` helpers, so it was inconsistent (or crashed) when numexpr was unavailable.

## Fix (all in `source/pyFAI/units.py`)

- Corrected `rotation_tilt_angle` to the beam-axis rotation with the right sign and updated `formula_qhorz_rot` / `formula_qvert_rot` to match (incident about `x`, then tilt about `z`).
- Made `eq_scattering_angle_*` and `eq_exit_angle_*` apply `rotate_sample_orientation` in the numpy path, matching the numexpr formulas.
- Made `q_lab_horz`, `q_lab_vert`, `q_lab_beam` use `numpy.cos`/`numpy.sin` so the numpy path works on arrays.
- Reworked `_update_ne_equation` to always rebuild from `formula_so1` for every orientation (including 1) and compute the numexpr signature from the final substituted formula.

## Verification

- `python reproduce.py` completes and now shows the reciprocal-polar feature center moving consistently with the angle view (run A chi ≈ +0.6608, run B chi ≈ −0.5967; the angle view is unchanged).
- The corrected polar view was independently re-derived from the exit-angle geometry and matches exactly.
- End-to-end tests across all 8 orientations, several incident/tilt values, random asymmetric panels, 1D and 2D integrations, and both numexpr and numpy paths all pass.
- The patch was applied to a pristine copy of the repository and `reproduce.py` was re-run successfully.

The patch is at `<patch-omitted>`.
